analysis.one_liner: Ends federal price supports and supply limits that keep sugar prices high.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal the federal sugar price support program drew 119 cosponsors from both parties but never got a vote, dying in a House Agriculture subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the federal sugar program: the government loans that guarantee sugar growers a minimum price, plus the marketing quotas and acreage allotments that limit who can grow and sell sugar. It would bar the Agriculture Secretary from ever offering sugar price supports again through the Commodity Credit Corporation, with the changes taking effect October 1, 1996. Without those supports and supply limits, domestic sugar prices would be free to fall toward world levels.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who pay higher-than-world prices for sugar and sugary products under the current program, would see prices fall. Food manufacturers that use sugar as an input — candy, baking, cereal makers — would see costs drop. Taxpayers would no longer backstop government sugar loans, and the government would no longer risk accumulating sugar it bought to prop up prices.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sugar price support program, under which the Commodity Credit Corporation makes loans to sugar beet and sugarcane growers at guaranteed price levels, ending the federal guarantee that keeps their returns above market prices [S3].
Repeals the marketing quotas and acreage allotments that restrict how much sugar can be marketed and who can grow it, ending the supply controls that restrict competition [S3].

Prohibits the Secretary of Agriculture from providing any future price support for sugar beets or sugarcane through loans, payments, or purchases, so the program could not be quietly rebuilt by the department, while honoring loans already outstanding [S3].
Sets a clean effective date of October 1, 1996 and preserves existing liabilities, so growers would finish out their commitments without grandfathered loopholes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors, who would lose guaranteed minimum prices, government purchase backstops, and protection from competition. Sugar-producing regions — Florida, Louisiana, the Red River Valley — would bear the adjustment as their crops sold at world prices instead of supported prices.

drawbacks.text: Ending the loan program would expose beet and cane growers to world sugar prices, which are themselves depressed by heavily subsidized foreign producers, and some growers could not survive the transition, with job losses concentrated in sugar-producing towns [S3].

The program's defenders argue it operates at no net cost to taxpayers because growers repay their loans, so the case for repeal rests on the higher prices consumers pay — a diffuse benefit spread across grocery bills that growers individually feel as a direct income loss [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are broad but diffuse: every household that buys sugar or sugary food pays the program's hidden premium, while the losses are concentrated and visible on a few thousand farms. On paper that trade favors repeal. The bill's weakness is that it offers no transition assistance for growers who made planting and land decisions in reliance on the program, which is the strongest good-faith argument its opponents had — and the reason an Agriculture Committee dominated by farm-state members gave it no hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and its specialty crops subcommittee, which never held a markup or let it reach the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Dan Miller of Florida introduced the bill on May 23, 1995 with 85 original cosponsors from both parties [S1].
It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee the same day, and three days later to the Subcommittee on Risk Management and Specialty Crops, the standard path to a quiet death [S5].
By the end of 1995 it had 119 cosponsors — 48 Democrats and 71 Republicans — but the subcommittee and full committee never acted on it [S4].
The sponsor gave introductory remarks in September 1995, and no markup, vote, or floor action ever followed before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar cane and beet growers kept the price supports and supply limits that hold their returns above world market prices, and consumers kept paying the premium.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers, who kept their program

for.name: Dan Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan cosponsor list; gave introductory remarks on the floor in September 1995

for.name: 71 of 236 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Majority Leader Dick Armey

for.name: 48 of 198 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Chuck Schumer of New York

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Chairman Pat Roberts (R-KS) and the committee's leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or a vote on the bill, leaving it to die in the Risk Management and Specialty Crops subcommittee

against.name: Sugar cane and beet growers
against.role: Growers and processors, organized nationally and in Florida, Louisiana, and the sugar beet states
against.what_they_did: Defended the price support and supply control program during the 1995-96 farm bill debate, and the farm bill written by the Agriculture Committee kept the sugar program intact

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 48 Democrats and 71 Republicans cosponsored — but the bill never reached a recorded vote, so the opposition that killed it in committee was never measured on the floor.

industries.industry: Sugar cane and beet growers and processors
industries.note: The program is the industry's guarantee: government loans at supported price levels plus marketing quotas and acreage allotments keep domestic sugar prices above world levels. Repeal would end both the price floor and the supply controls, so the industry's interest runs directly against consumers who pay the premium.
Manufacturers pay above-world prices for sugar under the program, which is why some candy and food production has moved abroad. Repeal would lower their input costs, in line with what consumers want.

industries.industry: Taxpayers via the Commodity Credit Corporation
industries.note: The CCC would no longer backstop sugar loans or risk accumulating sugar to prop up prices; the bill specifically bars the Secretary from using CCC funds for sugar price supports.
